title: Job Scheduler
summary: Simulate a batch job scheduler for a data platform, adding the features real orchestrators need.

stages.title: Worker pool
stages.requirement:
We're simulating the scheduler behind our batch platform. Implement
`Scheduler(workers=1)`:

- `submit(job_id, duration)` queues a job (`duration >= 1` time units). A duplicate
  `job_id` raises `ValueError`.
- `run()` simulates execution from time 0 and returns `(job_id, start, end)` for every
  job, sorted by `start`, then `job_id`.

Jobs are assigned in **submission order**. Each job goes to the worker that becomes free
**earliest**, and on ties the lowest-numbered worker (workers are numbered `0..workers-1`).
A worker runs one job at a time.

```python
s = Scheduler(workers=2)
s.submit("a", 3); s.submit("b", 2); s.submit("c", 1)
s.run()  # -> [("a", 0, 3), ("b", 0, 2), ("c", 2, 3)]
```

hiddenTests.name: test_large

def test_large():
    s = Scheduler(workers=4)
    for i in range(20_000):
        s.submit(f"j{i:05d}", (i % 5) + 1)
    out = s.run()
    assert len(out) == 20_000
    # 60,000 units of work on 4 workers: greedy assignment finishes at 15,002.
    assert max(end for _, _, end in out) == 15_002

hints: At each step you need the worker that frees up earliest. Which data structure gives you the minimum quickly?
A min-heap of `(free_at, worker_id)` handles both rules: earliest free, then lowest id.

solution.explanation:
A min-heap of `(free_at, worker)` assigns each job, in submission order, to the
earliest-available worker. The tuple ordering breaks ties by worker number for free.
Each assignment is O(log w). Sorting the output at the end matches the required
order.
solution.timeComplexity: O(n log w + n log n)

stages.title: Dependencies
stages.requirement:
Nice. Real pipelines have dependencies. `submit` gains `depends_on=()`, an iterable of
job ids that must **finish** before this job can **start**.

- Jobs become **ready** when all their dependencies have finished. Whenever workers are
  free, ready jobs are assigned in **submission order**, to free workers in increasing
  worker number. A job that becomes ready at time `t` can start at `t`.
- `run()` raises `ValueError` if a dependency names an unknown job or the dependencies
  contain a cycle. Dependencies may be submitted in any order.
- Output is unchanged: `(job_id, start, end)` sorted by start, then id.

```python
s = Scheduler(workers=2)
s.submit("extract", 2)
s.submit("transform", 3, depends_on=["extract"])
s.submit("report", 1)
s.run()  # -> [("extract", 0, 2), ("report", 0, 1), ("transform", 2, 5)]
```

hints: Assigning jobs in a fixed order no longer works. You need to simulate time: events happen when jobs finish.

Keep a min-heap of running jobs by end time, a heap of idle worker ids, and a heap of ready jobs keyed by submission index. Advance time to the next completion, free those workers and release dependents.
Validate first: unknown ids, then a topological check (Kahn's algorithm) for cycles.

solution.explanation:
Dependencies force a real **discrete-event simulation**. Time jumps to the next job
completion, completions free workers and release dependents whose last dependency
just finished, and then idle workers take ready jobs in submission order. Stage 1's
behavior is the special case with no dependencies, so its tests still pass. Kahn's
algorithm validates the graph up front.

stages.title: Retries with backoff
stages.requirement:
Jobs fail in production. Model failures deterministically:

- `submit(..., fail_attempts=0, max_retries=0)`: the first `fail_attempts` attempts of the
  job **fail**. An attempt takes the full `duration` either way.
- The constructor takes `base_backoff=1`. After failed attempt number `k` (1-based), if the
  job has retries left (`k <= max_retries`), it becomes ready again at
  `failure_time + base_backoff * 2**(k-1)`. Otherwise it is **failed**, and every job that
  depends on it, directly or transitively, is **skipped** and never runs.
- `run()` returns only **successful** attempts as `(job_id, start, end)`.
- New `report()` returns `{job_id: {"status": "succeeded" | "failed" | "skipped",
  "attempts": n}}` for the last `run()`. Before any `run()`, it raises `RuntimeError`.

```python
s = Scheduler(workers=1, base_backoff=1)
s.submit("flaky", 2, fail_attempts=1, max_retries=1)
s.run()      # -> [("flaky", 3, 5)]   (fails 0-2, backs off 1, retries 3-5)
s.report()   # -> {"flaky": {"status": "succeeded", "attempts": 2}}
```

test_failure_skips_dependents
visibleTests.code:
def test_failure_skips_dependents():
    s = Scheduler(workers=2)
    s.submit("load", 1, fail_attempts=5, max_retries=1)
    s.submit("model", 1, depends_on=["load"])
    s.submit("dash", 1, depends_on=["model"])
    s.submit("other", 1)
    assert s.run() == [("other", 0, 1)]
    assert s.report() == {
        "load": {"status": "failed", "attempts": 2},
        "model": {"status": "skipped", "attempts": 0},
        "dash": {"status": "skipped", "attempts": 0},
        "other": {"status": "succeeded", "attempts": 1},
    }

hints: A failed attempt doesn't release dependents. It either re-enters the queue later or ends the job.
Add a second heap of `(ready_at, job)` for jobs in backoff. The next event time is the earlier of the next completion and the next backoff expiry.
On permanent failure, walk the dependents graph to mark everything downstream as skipped. Record attempts per job for `report()`.

solution.explanation:
The simulation gains a third event source: jobs in backoff, kept in a heap by
`ready_at`. The clock now advances to the earlier of the next completion and the next
backoff expiry. A completion either succeeds (releasing dependents), schedules a
retry with exponential delay, or fails permanently and marks the transitive
downstream as skipped. Per-job attempt counts feed `report()`.
solution.timeComplexity: O((n * r + e) log n) for r attempts per job

stages.title: Priorities
stages.requirement:
Last one. Some jobs are urgent. `submit(..., priority=0)`: among **ready** jobs, higher
`priority` runs first, and equal priorities keep submission order. Priority never preempts
a running job, and a job keeps its priority when it retries.

```python
s = Scheduler(workers=1)
s.submit("batch", 2)
s.submit("backfill", 2)
s.submit("hotfix", 1, priority=10)
s.run()  # -> [("hotfix", 0, 1), ("batch", 1, 3), ("backfill", 3, 5)]
```

hiddenTests.name: test_large_priority_mix

hints: Only the ordering of the ready set changes.
Key the ready heap by `(-priority, submission_index)` instead of just the submission index, and use the same key when a retry re-enters the queue.

solution.explanation:
The ready queue's ordering key becomes `(-priority, submission_index)`, used both for
jobs released by dependencies and for retries leaving backoff, so priority survives
retries. Running jobs are never interrupted, because priority only affects which
ready job an idle worker takes. With a priority of 0 everywhere, behavior is exactly
stage 3's.
